newsitem.title: USA: Emerging markets to thrive from Fed policy-experts.
newsitem.headline: Emerging markets to thrive from Fed policy-experts.

text.p: The climate of steady U.S. interest rates should extend the stunning rally in emerging market bond prices, although Brady bonds may face a healthy correction ahead, U.S. analysts said.
The Federal Reserve on Tuesday left its key federal funds rate steady at 5.25 percent, defying market expectations and justifying the optimism for emerging market assets.
"It validates the trends we've seen over the past few weeks of a strong influx of capital to the emerging markets," said Chase Securities Inc's senior economist Jos Barrionuevo.
Steady U.S. interest rates should mean that U.S. and international investors would continue to seek out the emerging markets for high returns.

Over the past nine months, vast amounts of fresh money -- much of it from U.S. institutional investors "crossing over" from other markets -- has boosted Brady bond prices and led developing nations to explore new ways of refinancing debt.

"This is a short-term boost to the market, but fundamentally the market for emerging market bonds is much deeper, better based (than in the past)," said Arturo Porzecanski, chief economist at ING Barings.

As of Monday the JP Morgan emerging market bond composite index had risen about 27-1/2 percent year-to-date, with more that 23 percent in Latin American assets and close to 43 percent growth in non-Latins.
With no increase in U.S. rates, analysts expected the strength in Brady bonds to persist, albeit in a more circumspect environment.
"What this signals is that the upward trend will continue, but I think the market is going to be a little more cautious than in the past," Barrionuevo said.
The markets will be seeking to determine whether the U.S. central bank may take stronger action in the future to make up for its current steady policy, he said.

Porzecanski warned that the Brady bond market might undergo a correction in the fourth quarter, and counselled that investors procure some insurance by buying puts, selling calls, or purchasing barrier options.
As emerging nations have become more creditworthy and found ways to issue debt less expensively, they have become less subject to the whims of Fed policy, analysts said.
Still, the shadow of this Fed meeting had loomed large over Latin American and other emerging markets.

"Latin America should be rejoicing," said Lawrence Krohn, Latin American economist at UBS Securities. "If the Fed had had raised rates it probably would have gone 1/4 point and would not have changed things fundamentally, but it would have soured the mood."
Unchanged Fed policy may also allow more emerging nations to follow the lead of Mexico and the Philippines, which convinced investors to exchange their Brady debt for uncollateralized global bonds.

Such swaps permit nations to retire Brady bonds, named for the former U.S. Treasury Secretary Nicholas Brady's plan to restructure defaulted commercial bank borrowings from the 1980s, and to free the underlying U.S. Treasury collateral.
"This market has arrived," said Arturo Porzecanski, chief economist at ING Barings. "While it can have a correction, the outlook medium term is very favorable."
